headline: Global wheat supply through peak harvest season to fall ~30% due to Russia-Ukraine conflict; Egypt, Tunisia and other import-dependent developing economies most exposed
reasoning: Wheat exports from Russia and Ukraine have dropped approximately 70% year-on-year. Looking at the total global basket of wheat being loaded onto vessels, I'Anson expects a roughly 30% loss in supply through the peak harvest season running to October. Rich developed economies like Europe will absorb higher prices, but import-dependent economies in North Africa and the Middle East — with limited fiscal and monetary buffers — face severe food security risk if grain availability problems persist, which he expects they will.
quote: Crop exports, wheat exports out of Russia, Ukraine are precipitously dropping. They've dropped 70%, excuse me, from year-earlier levels. And if you look at just the total global basket of wheat exports that are getting loaded onto vessels, we're likely going to see a 30% loss in supply through this peak harvest season, which lasts through October. The issues in Russia, Ukraine are significant. And it's really going to have the biggest impact on your developing import dependent economies like Egypt and Tunisia, these big import dependent economies that have limited fiscal and monetary buffers. Right places like Europe — they'll import that grain when needed. They'll pay the higher price. But places in North Africa and also across places in the Middle East as well, quite exposed.

headline: Crude flows through Strait of Hormuz recovering from March-May lows but still below pre-war levels; real constraint is global refinery capacity down ~6 million barrels per day across Middle East, Russia and China
reasoning: Reid I'Anson notes that crude flows through the Strait of Hormuz have picked up relative to March-April-May peaks of conflict intensity, but remain below pre-war levels. The more pressing issue is that global refinery runs are severely constrained: Middle East refineries have cut 2.5 million barrels per day versus a February baseline, Russian refineries are down more than 1 million barrels per day due to the Russia-Ukraine war, and China has voluntarily cut 2.5 million barrels per day to limit crude imports. This means the crude market is not heavily undersupplied on its own, but refined product availability is critically tight.
quote: The market right now is really picking up on the refinery availability problem, right? We are seeing crude flows out of the Middle East happen steadily. Certainly not back to pre-war levels, but we are really facing constraints in refinery runs globally, refinery capacity not only in the Middle East, which has had to cut refinery runs by 2.5 million barrels per day against the February baseline. We're also seeing the Russia-Ukraine war hit Russian refinery runs. You know you're looking at more than a million offline there. And then of course, China has elected to cut refinery runs as well in a bid to limit crude demand and crude imports. And so that's another 2.5 million barrels per day of cuts there. So while the crude market is not necessarily heavily under supplied, it's because refinery runs are pretty constrained right now.
episode_title: The energy shock moving beyond the pump

headline: Energy and food price shock set to be highly inflationary through year-end, forcing central banks into limited rate hikes despite resilient real growth in developed economies
reasoning: The combination of elevated diesel prices feeding into food production costs, alongside Black Sea disruptions cutting wheat exports from Russia and Ukraine, creates a compounding inflationary shock. I'Anson expects the global economy — particularly developed economies — to show resilience in real growth terms, but inflation will be a persistent problem that forces central banks to hike rates at least to a limited degree. The pressure will be most acutely felt by import-dependent developing economies like Egypt and Tunisia that lack fiscal and monetary buffers.
quote: Diesel flows into a lot of other goods. Um, you know, food production, for example. And that's already being compounded. The issue in the food side of the grains in particular, is being compounded by issues in the Black Sea. Right. So you've got higher diesel prices, raises the cost to produce crops. We've got issues in the Black Sea, i.e. Russia, Ukraine struggling to get wheat out of that region. And so it's very inflationary. And I think into the end of the year that's going to kind of be the narrative. I think the global economy is going to show a degree of resilience, especially among your developed economies, in terms of real growth. But there's going to be an inflation problem, and that's going to put central banks in a corner where they have to at least hike rates to a limited degree.
episode_title: The energy shock moving beyond the pump

headline: Crack spreads at or near record highs — diesel up 90% and gasoline up 60% since late February versus Brent up only 30%, revealing severe crude-to-product dislocation showing up at the US pump
reasoning: Petroleum product prices have massively outpaced crude: New York Harbor low-sulfur diesel is up 90% from a February 28th baseline while Brent crude is up only 30%, and the RBOB gasoline contract is up 60% since late February. Heating oil on the East Coast is testing 2022 highs seen when the Russia-Ukraine war first broke out. This dislocation between crude and products is materialising at the US pump and is creating a significant political problem for the Trump administration heading into the midterms.
quote: You're seeing this in crack spreads. They're massive. They're at record high levels or near record highs for diesel and pretty elevated for gasoline as well. I was looking at a chart of just front month New York Harbor LSD prices against a February 28th baseline. They're up 90%. Right. You compare that to Brent, which is up, you know, 30%. Right. And so that's kind of revealing the differential in crude versus product availability. But even stuff like RBOB, which is the gasoline contract in the United States, those prices are up 60% since late February. So there is a real dislocation between crude and products. And that is showing up at the pump here in the United States.

headline: Refinery crack spreads at historically extreme levels due to simultaneous outages in the Middle East, Russia, and deliberate Chinese run cuts — petroleum product prices will not fall as fast as crude
reasoning: Following the MOU in mid-June, crude flowed back into the market but diesel crack spreads surged to around $90/barrel versus $25-30 a year earlier, with gasoline margins similarly elevated. Refinery outages in the Middle East are estimated at around 2 million barrels per day, Russian refinery throughput is down approximately 1.4 million barrels per day due to Ukrainian attacks, and Chinese refinery runs are estimated to be off 2.7-3 million barrels per day due to deliberate cuts in crude imports. These three concurrent drivers are keeping petroleum product margins elevated, meaning declines in crude prices will not translate proportionally to declines in refined product prices until refinery infrastructure recovers.
quote: We saw uh, crack spreads which are effectively refinery margins surged to some of the highest levels we've ever seen. You know, diesel margins were at 90 bucks, right? So that again, uh, this time last year, you were sitting at 25, 30 bucks a barrel for that margin. Uh, same kind of story across the gasoline. A little bit less extreme, but still the same kind of margin story across gasoline. Reason being the year we have a refinery capacity problem, not only in the Middle East, you know, which is, you know, we estimate outages across the Middle East for refinery runs of around 2 million barrels per day. But this also extends to the Ukraine Russia conflict as well. Ukraine has been attacking Russian, Russian refinery runs. You know, Russian refinery throughput is likely down by around 1.4 million barrels per day. So that's another key critical piece that's impacting the product side of the story. Lastly, you have China. China is a little different, unlike the Middle East and Russia, which kind of you know, they didn't have any choice on their refinery run situation in China. They have chosen to cut runs and cut crude imports as a result. And so we estimate that Chinese refinery runs likely off 2.7 to 3 million barrels per day.

headline: Kpler's Reid I'Anson sees a persistent divergence between crude oil price declines and petroleum product prices as refinery infrastructure lags
reasoning: Reid I'Anson argues that while crude oil prices have been declining, petroleum product prices (gasoline, diesel) will not fall at the same pace because refinery infrastructure has not caught up. US Gulf Coast and European refiners are running at maximum capacity, which sustains a wedge between crude and refined product prices. This 'tale of two oil markets' dichotomy is expected to persist for some time.
quote: The price declines are probably not going to match the kind of declines you see on crude for now, not until refinery infrastructure catches up. And even when you look at places like the United States, you know, US Gulf Coast refiners are, you know, they're running as hard as they can right now. Same story in Europe. So, um, this kind of dichotomy between crude and products, I think, is a story that's going to continue for a while.

The key unresolved question is whether the White House will accept an arrangement allowing Iran to control the Strait and potentially charge tolls, which up to this point the US has been unwilling to concede. Reports of US military stockpile pressures may push Trump toward an agreement, but the outcome remains highly uncertain.
quote: Over the last several months, it looks like right now Iran and Oman are talking, the United States and Iran are talking. Hopefully we get some kind of agreement. Um, kind of on a level set here, though, at least on the data side of things, the Strait of Hormuz remains largely closed. And that's a big change from the initial period following the signing of the MOU in mid-June. We did see a surge in volumes of of crude leaving the Middle East, say, in that second half of June, first week of July period, we were seeing 9 to 10 million barrels per day exit. Uh, that has dramatically declined. We're sitting at around 2.5 million barrels per day of crude leaving the strait right now. So, you know, I think that the critical, you know, part to watch is what are physical flows doing through the Strait of Hormuz as you try and navigate this back and forth set of headlines.

However, inflation is the bigger concern, with global inflation expected to be about 80bps above pre-conflict forecasts and US core and headline inflation running well above target.
